points: Feed: straight-run naphtha, research octane number 64.0.
Conditions held constant across the runs: pressure 1.4 megapascals, liquid hourly space velocity 2.8 per hour, hydrogen-to-hydrocarbon molar ratio 5.2.
Severity was set by reactor inlet temperature: 490 degrees Celsius at low severity, 515 degrees Celsius at high severity.
Product research octane number reached 98.2 at high severity and 91.4 at low severity.
Aromatics content of the reformate was 68.4 % by mass at high severity and 57.9 % by mass at low severity.
Liquid yield was 82.6 % by mass at high severity and 87.3 % by mass at low severity.
Benzene in the high-severity reformate was 0.8 % by volume, against a specification limit of 1.0 % by volume.
Octane values are means of triplicate determinations; the standard deviation of a determination was 0.6 octane units.
Octane decline over the stability run was 1.8 octane units over 400 hours on stream.
definitions: research octane number = a standardised measure of a fuel's resistance to knock, determined on a test engine under the research method
liquid hourly space velocity = the volumetric liquid feed rate divided by the catalyst volume, stated per hour
severity = the operating intensity of the reformer, set in this work by reactor inlet temperature
limits: The octane and benzene claims hold for feeds with a sulphur content below 10 milligrams per kilogram.
figures: Fig. 1: research octane number against reactor inlet temperature at the two severity levels
prose:
Reformate octane performance was measured on a pilot catalytic reformer operated at two severity levels. The catalyst was a platinum-on-alumina formulation held in a fixed bed, and the bed had completed a standard regeneration before the campaign opened. The feed was a straight-run naphtha (research octane number 64.0), and sampling at each condition began after line-out at the separator outlet. Pressure (1.4 megapascals), liquid hourly space velocity (2.8 per hour) and hydrogen-to-hydrocarbon molar ratio (5.2) held constant across the runs. Reactor inlet temperature set the severity level (490 degrees Celsius at low severity, 515 degrees Celsius at high severity).
Product research octane number reached 98.2 at high severity (91.4 at low severity), and the octane gain tracked the aromatics content of the reformate (68.4 % by mass at high severity, 57.9 % by mass at low severity). Aromatisation reactions carry the gain: dehydrogenation of naphthenes and dehydrocyclisation of paraffins raise the aromatics fraction, and the aromatics fraction carries the knock resistance of the blend. Liquid yield moved against octane (82.6 % by mass at high severity, 87.3 % by mass at low severity), and hydrocracking at the higher temperature priced the octane gain in liquid product. Benzene in the high-severity reformate was 0.8 % by volume, inside a specification limit of 1.0 % by volume. Octane values are means of triplicate determinations, and the standard deviation of a determination was 0.6 octane units. The high-severity product held octane across the stability run, with a decline of 1.8 octane units over 400 hours on stream. For feeds with a sulphur content below 10 milligrams per kilogram, the high-severity condition delivered a reformate at the higher octane level inside the benzene specification (Fig. 1). The trade-off between octane and liquid yield sets the operating choice for a commercial unit, and the choice turns on the price spread between high-octane blendstock and liquid product volume in the market served.

points: Wetland: horizontal subsurface-flow bed, surface area 850 square metres, gravel bed depth 0.6 metres.
Hydraulic loading rate 0.12 metres per day; nominal hydraulic retention time 5.5 days.
Influent total phosphorus averaged 6.8 milligrams per litre; effluent total phosphorus averaged 1.9 milligrams per litre; removal 72 %.
Effluent values are means over 14 monthly campaigns; standard deviation of the monthly effluent means 0.4 milligrams per litre.
Winter performance: effluent total phosphorus 2.6 milligrams per litre; removal 62 %.
Harvested above-ground biomass accounted for 18 % of the phosphorus load removed over the year.
definitions: total phosphorus = the phosphorus concentration of an unfiltered sample after digestion, stated as elemental phosphorus
hydraulic retention time = the water volume of the bed divided by the volumetric flow rate through the bed
hydraulic loading rate = the volumetric inflow divided by the surface area of the bed
limits: The removal claim holds for influent total phosphorus at or above 4.0 milligrams per litre.
figures: Fig. 1: monthly influent and effluent total phosphorus concentrations across the sampling year
prose:
Phosphorus removal was measured in a horizontal subsurface-flow constructed wetland treating settled municipal wastewater. The bed was planted with common reed over a gravel matrix, and flow passed below the gravel surface along the full length of the bed. The wetland had a surface area of 850 square metres and a gravel bed depth of 0.6 metres, and the hydraulic loading rate was 0.12 metres per day (nominal hydraulic retention time 5.5 days). Sampling points stood at the inlet distribution chamber and at the outlet collection chamber, and total phosphorus was measured by colorimetry after digestion of unfiltered samples.
Influent total phosphorus averaged 6.8 milligrams per litre, and effluent total phosphorus averaged 1.9 milligrams per litre (removal 72 % across the wetland). Effluent values are means over 14 monthly campaigns, and the standard deviation of the monthly effluent means was 0.4 milligrams per litre. Removal weakened in winter. Effluent total phosphorus rose to 2.6 milligrams per litre in the winter campaigns, and removal fell to 62 %. The seasonal pattern followed plant dormancy and falling water temperature: plant uptake slowed, microbial activity in the rhizosphere slowed, and sorption onto the gravel carried a larger share of a smaller removal. Harvested above-ground biomass accounted for 18 % of the phosphorus load removed over the year, and the harvested fraction left the system in the cut material. The balance of the removed load stayed in the bed, held by sorption and accretion in the gravel matrix. For influent total phosphorus at or above 4.0 milligrams per litre, the wetland held the stated removal across all seasons sampled (Fig. 1). A second bed operated in parallel received the same wastewater, and the two beds agreed on the seasonal pattern while differing in the depth of the winter decline. Design values taken from the campaign belong to the loading range of the bed as built, and a bed loaded beyond that range carries a shorter contact time per unit of flow.

points: The extract was frozen at minus 40 degrees Celsius and held until the full charge reached shelf temperature.
Primary drying ran at a chamber pressure of 12 pascals for 38 hours.
Secondary drying raised the shelf to 30 degrees Celsius for 8 hours.
Residual moisture after primary drying alone was 4.6 % by mass; after secondary drying the residual moisture was 1.8 % by mass.
Residual moisture values are means across 6 vials per batch; the standard deviation was 0.3 percentage points.
After storage for 90 days at 25 degrees Celsius in sealed vials, residual moisture rose to 2.4 % by mass.
Reconstitution time in warm water was 45 seconds.
definitions: residual moisture = the mass of water remaining in the dried product divided by the dry solids mass, stated as a percentage
primary drying = the stage in which ice leaves the frozen product by sublimation under vacuum
secondary drying = the stage in which bound water leaves the dried matrix at raised shelf temperature
limits: The residual moisture claim holds for a fill depth of 10 millimetres in the vial.
figures: Fig. 1: residual moisture by drying stage for the programme with secondary drying and the programme without
prose:
Residual moisture was measured for a coffee extract freeze-dried under a programme with a secondary drying stage and a programme that ended after primary drying. The extract was frozen at minus 40 degrees Celsius and held until the full charge reached shelf temperature. Primary drying ran at a chamber pressure of 12 pascals for 38 hours, with the sublimation front moving from the vial top toward the base as the dried layer thickened. Secondary drying raised the shelf to 30 degrees Celsius for 8 hours. Residual moisture was measured by Karl Fischer titration, a coulometric method that reacts water in the sample with a reagent and counts the charge consumed.
Residual moisture after primary drying alone was 4.6 % by mass, and after secondary drying the residual moisture was 1.8 % by mass (Fig. 1). Residual moisture values are means across 6 vials per batch, and the standard deviation was 0.3 percentage points. The gap between the two programmes sits in the bound water of the dried matrix: primary drying removes ice by sublimation and leaves adsorbed water in place, and the raised shelf temperature of secondary drying supplies the energy that desorbs the bound fraction. Cake structure held across both programmes, with no collapse, no shrinkage from the fill line and no melt-back at the vial base. After storage for 90 days at 25 degrees Celsius in sealed vials, residual moisture rose to 2.4 % by mass, and the rise records moisture ingress through the stopper rather than a change in the cake. Reconstitution time in warm water was 45 seconds for the secondary-dried product, and the reconstituted extract carried no undissolved solids. For a fill depth of 10 millimetres in the vial, the programme with secondary drying delivered the lower residual moisture at the cost of the added shelf time.

points: Current density was run at 450 amperes per square metre and at 600 amperes per square metre.
The electrolyte carried zinc at 55 grams per litre and sulphuric acid at 160 grams per litre, at 38 degrees Celsius.
Current efficiency reached 91.2 % at the lower current density and 84.6 % at the higher current density.
Cell voltage was 3.4 volts at the lower current density and 3.8 volts at the higher current density.
Energy consumption at the lower current density was 3.06 kilowatt-hours per kilogram of zinc deposited.
A cobalt addition trial gave a current efficiency of 78.3 % with cobalt at 0.4 milligrams per litre.
Deposits were harvested on a 24 hour cycle.
Current efficiency values are means over 5 cells; the standard deviation was 1.1 percentage points.
definitions: current efficiency = the charge carried by zinc deposition divided by the total charge passed, stated as a percentage
current density = the cell current divided by the cathode area
electrowinning = the electrodeposition of a metal from a leach electrolyte in an electrolytic cell
limits: The efficiency claim holds for electrolyte with iron below 2 milligrams per litre.
figures: Fig. 1: current efficiency and cell voltage against current density
prose:
Current efficiency was measured in pilot zinc electrowinning cells run at two current density levels with a synthetic electrolyte. Cathodes were aluminium blanks and anodes were a lead-silver alloy, and deposits were stripped, washed, dried and weighed at the end of each cycle. Current density was run at 450 amperes per square metre and at 600 amperes per square metre. The electrolyte carried zinc at 55 grams per litre and sulphuric acid at 160 grams per litre, at 38 degrees Celsius.
Current efficiency reached 91.2 % at the lower current density and 84.6 % at the higher current density (Fig. 1). Cell voltage was 3.4 volts at the lower current density and 3.8 volts at the higher current density. Energy consumption at the lower current density was 3.06 kilowatt-hours per kilogram of zinc deposited. The efficiency loss at the higher current density sits in hydrogen evolution at the cathode: a larger share of the charge reduces protons rather than zinc ions, and the deposit at the higher current density grew rougher, with nodules at the blank edges where local current density peaks. A cobalt addition trial gave a current efficiency of 78.3 % with cobalt at 0.4 milligrams per litre, and cobalt acts on the same route, catalysing hydrogen evolution on the deposit surface. Deposits were harvested on a 24 hour cycle. Current efficiency values are means over 5 cells, and the standard deviation was 1.1 percentage points. For electrolyte with iron below 2 milligrams per litre, the lower current density delivered the higher efficiency at the lower energy consumption. The operating choice between the two current density levels trades efficiency against tankhouse throughput, and a plant running at the higher level passes more metal per cell per day while paying for the gain in energy and in deposit quality. Electrolyte purification carries the cobalt result: cobalt control upstream of the cells protects the efficiency recorded at either level.

points: Factors and levels: temperature at 160 degrees Celsius (low) and 180 degrees Celsius (high); catalyst loading at 1 % by mass (low) and 3 % by mass (high).
Run yields, in percent: low temperature with low catalyst 42; high temperature with low catalyst 55; low temperature with high catalyst 48; high temperature with high catalyst 66.
Main effect of temperature: 15.5 percentage points of yield.
Main effect of catalyst loading: 8.5 percentage points of yield.
Interaction effect: 2.5 percentage points of yield.
Mean of the corner yields: 52.75 %; centre-point yield 53 %.
definitions: factorial design = an experiment in which every level of each factor is run in combination with every level of each other factor
main effect = the change in the mean response when a factor moves from its low level to its high level, averaged over the levels of the other factors
interaction = the change in the effect of one factor between the levels of another factor, stated at half the difference by the convention of a two-level design
centre point = a run at the midpoint of every factor range, used to test for curvature
limits: The effect estimates hold inside the factor ranges tested; a two-level design does not map curvature away from the centre point.
prose:
This tutorial builds a two-level factorial design for a reactor study and reads the factor effects from the completed runs. You end with three effect estimates and a curvature check, and you need a response measured at every corner of the design before the arithmetic starts. The response here is yield, and the factors are temperature and catalyst loading.
Set the levels first. Temperature runs at 160 degrees Celsius (low) and 180 degrees Celsius (high), and catalyst loading runs at 1 % by mass (low) and 3 % by mass (high). Run every combination, and randomise the run order where the apparatus allows the order to vary: run order confounds drift with factor effects when the runs follow the table order. The completed yields, in percent, were: low temperature with low catalyst 42; high temperature with low catalyst 55; low temperature with high catalyst 48; high temperature with high catalyst 66.
Average the yields at each level of a factor to read the main effect of that factor. The main effect of temperature was 15.5 percentage points of yield: raising temperature raised yield across both catalyst loadings. The main effect of catalyst loading was 8.5 percentage points of yield. Compare the temperature effect at each catalyst loading to read the interaction. The interaction effect was 2.5 percentage points of yield, small against the two main effects, and the small interaction marks a response that the two factors move near-additively across the tested ranges. Check the design with a centre point before extending the ranges. The mean of the corner yields was 52.75 %, and the centre-point yield was 53 %; the centre point sits on the corner mean, and curvature inside the ranges is negligible at the precision of the runs. The effect estimates hold inside the factor ranges tested; a two-level design does not map curvature away from the centre point, and a search for an optimum beyond the corners needs a design that maps the curvature.

points: Dry air flow to the tower: 2.5 kilograms of dry air per second.
Inlet humidity ratio 0.008 kilograms of water per kilogram of dry air; target outlet humidity ratio 0.020 kilograms per kilogram.
Evaporation rate required by the water balance: 0.030 kilograms per second.
Inlet dry-bulb temperature 40 degrees Celsius; outlet dry-bulb temperature 27 degrees Celsius at the design approach to saturation.
The flooding-checked gas velocity gives a packing cross-section of 3.1 square metres and a tower diameter of 2.0 metres.
Number of transfer units for the duty: 2.4; height of a transfer unit 0.9 metres; packed height 2.16 metres.
Packing pressure drop 180 pascals per metre of packed height; total gas-side pressure drop 389 pascals.
definitions: humidity ratio = the mass of water vapour divided by the mass of dry air in the gas stream
number of transfer units = a dimensionless count of the transfer duty, calculated from the change in humidity ratio and the mean driving force
height of a transfer unit = the packed height that performs one transfer unit of duty, taken from packing test data at the design liquid rate
transfer unit = one unit of transfer duty in the count that sizes the packed height
limits: The sizing holds for adiabatic operation with negligible heat loss through the tower wall.
prose:
This tutorial sizes a packed humidification tower that raises the humidity of an air stream by contact with recirculated water. You finish with a tower diameter, a packed height and a gas-side pressure drop. You need the gas flow, the inlet state of the air and the target outlet humidity before the sizing starts.
Start from the water balance. The dry air flow to the tower is 2.5 kilograms of dry air per second. The inlet humidity ratio is 0.008 kilograms of water per kilogram of dry air, and the target outlet humidity ratio is 0.020 kilograms per kilogram. The evaporation rate required by the water balance is 0.030 kilograms per second, and the make-up water line must supply the evaporation rate plus the blowdown stream. The inlet dry-bulb temperature is 40 degrees Celsius, and the outlet dry-bulb temperature is 27 degrees Celsius at the design approach to saturation; evaporation cools the air toward the wet-bulb temperature as the humidity ratio climbs. Check the evaporation rate against the humidity change before sizing the packing: the rate follows from the dry air flow and the humidity ratio difference alone, and an error here propagates into every later quantity.
Set the diameter from the gas velocity. Keep the superficial velocity below the flooding velocity of the packing at the design liquid rate; flooding fills the packing with liquid and the pressure drop climbs without bound. The flooding-checked gas velocity gives a packing cross-section of 3.1 square metres and a tower diameter of 2.0 metres. Set the packed height from the transfer duty. The number of transfer units for the duty is 2.4, the height of a transfer unit is 0.9 metres, and the packed height is 2.16 metres. Close with the pressure drop. The packing pressure drop is 180 pascals per metre of packed height, and the total gas-side pressure drop is 389 pascals; the fan duty follows from the total. The sizing holds for adiabatic operation with negligible heat loss through the tower wall.

points: The body: a steel sphere of diameter 25 millimetres.
Steel properties: density 7800 kilograms per cubic metre; specific heat capacity 480 joules per kilogram kelvin; thermal conductivity 45 watts per metre kelvin.
Heat transfer coefficient at the sphere surface: 120 watts per square metre kelvin.
Characteristic length of the sphere: 4.17 millimetres, that is 0.00417 metres.
Biot number of the sphere: 0.011, against the lumped-model criterion of 0.1.
Initial sphere temperature 300 degrees Celsius; quench fluid at 20 degrees Celsius; target temperature 60 degrees Celsius.
Time constant of the sphere: 130 seconds.
The cooling calculation carries a logarithm term of 7 in the temperature ratio; cooling time to the target temperature: 253 seconds.
definitions: Biot number = the ratio of internal conduction resistance to surface convection resistance in a body, calculated as the heat transfer coefficient multiplied by the characteristic length and divided by the thermal conductivity
characteristic length = the volume of a body divided by its surface area
time constant = the product of density, characteristic length and specific heat capacity divided by the heat transfer coefficient, for a body cooled under the lumped capacitance model
lumped capacitance model = a transient conduction model that treats the temperature inside a body as uniform at each instant
limits: The cooling time holds while the heat transfer coefficient stays at the design value; boiling at the surface changes the coefficient and the time constant with it.
prose:
This tutorial estimates the cooling time of a hot steel sphere in a quench bath with the lumped capacitance model, and checks the model before trusting the estimate. You finish with a cooling time and with the validity check that licenses the time. You need the sphere size, the steel properties, the surface heat transfer coefficient and the two bath temperatures at the start.
Take the body and the properties first. The body is a steel sphere of diameter 25 millimetres. The steel properties are: density 7800 kilograms per cubic metre; specific heat capacity 480 joules per kilogram kelvin; thermal conductivity 45 watts per metre kelvin. The heat transfer coefficient at the sphere surface is 120 watts per square metre kelvin. The characteristic length of the sphere is 4.17 millimetres, that is 0.00417 metres; a sphere carries the largest volume-to-area ratio of the common shapes, and the characteristic length records that geometry in a single length.
Run the validity check before the cooling arithmetic. The Biot number of the sphere is 0.011, against the lumped-model criterion of 0.1. The Biot number sits an order of magnitude inside the criterion, and the temperature inside the sphere stays near-uniform during the quench: conduction inside the steel redistributes heat far faster than convection removes heat at the surface. A Biot number near the criterion withdraws that licence, and a body at the boundary needs a distributed conduction solution in place of the lumped model.
Carry the temperatures and the time constant into the cooling calculation. The initial sphere temperature is 300 degrees Celsius, the quench fluid stands at 20 degrees Celsius, and the target temperature is 60 degrees Celsius. The time constant of the sphere is 130 seconds. The cooling calculation carries a logarithm term of 7 in the temperature ratio, and the cooling time to the target temperature is 253 seconds. Read the result against the time constant: the sphere needs about two time constants to close most of the temperature gap, and the long tail of the exponential sets the last part of the wait. The cooling time holds while the heat transfer coefficient stays at the design value; boiling at the surface changes the coefficient and the time constant with it.

points: Peak external quantum efficiency: 21.4 %.
Brightness reached 8500 candelas per square metre at a current density of 10 milliamperes per square centimetre.
Operating time to half the initial luminance: 320 hours at an initial luminance of 1000 candelas per square metre, against 85 hours for the control device.
Emission peak at 520 nanometres, with a full width at half maximum of 24 nanometres.
Efficiency values are means over 18 devices; the standard deviation was 1.3 percentage points.
Turn-on voltage: 2.3 volts.
definitions: external quantum efficiency = the photons emitted from the device divided by the electrons injected, stated as a percentage
operating lifetime = the operating time at which the luminance of a device falls to half the initial value under constant current
turn-on voltage = the applied voltage at which a device reaches a set reference luminance
prose: Light-emitting diodes based on metal halide perovskite films are efficient emitters, and device lifetime under continuous operation has limited the material class in display applications. A mixed-cation perovskite emitter with a polymer interlayer at the hole-injection contact was fabricated and tested against a control device built without the interlayer. The interlayer device emitted in the green, with an emission peak at 520 nanometres and a full width at half maximum of 24 nanometres, and a turn-on voltage of 2.3 volts. Peak external quantum efficiency reached 21.4 %, and brightness reached 8500 candelas per square metre at a current density of 10 milliamperes per square centimetre. Efficiency values are means over 18 devices, and the standard deviation was 1.3 percentage points. The operating time to half the initial luminance was 320 hours at an initial luminance of 1000 candelas per square metre, against 85 hours for the control device. The interlayer suppresses ion migration at the contact, and the lifetime gain at equal efficiency assigns the dominant degradation route to the contact rather than the emitter bulk. Perovskite diodes with contact-side stabilisation meet the efficiency and lifetime levels that display backlight development requires, and the fabrication route uses solution coating throughout, a route that transfers to large-area substrates.

points: Operating temperature: 750 degrees Celsius.
Peak power density reached 1.12 watts per square centimetre, against 0.74 watts per square centimetre for the baseline cell.
Open-circuit voltage: 1.08 volts.
Area-specific resistance: 0.18 ohm square centimetres at the operating temperature.
At 0.7 volts the cell delivered a current density of 1.35 amperes per square centimetre.
Fuel utilisation in the performance test: 65 %.
Peak power fell by 3.8 % over 500 hours of operation.
Electrolyte thickness: 8 micrometres.
Power values are means over 6 cells; the standard deviation of peak power density was 0.05 watts per square centimetre.
definitions: area-specific resistance = the electrical resistance of a cell multiplied by the active cell area
peak power density = the maximum electrical power delivered per unit of active cell area across the current-voltage characteristic
open-circuit voltage = the cell voltage measured at zero drawn current
prose: Solid oxide fuel cells convert hydrogen and air directly into electricity at high temperature, and cell resistance sets the power available from a given cell area. An anode-supported cell with a thin electrolyte and a cobalt-free cathode was fabricated and tested against a baseline cell with a conventional cathode. The electrolyte thickness was 8 micrometres, and the operating temperature was 750 degrees Celsius. The test cell outperformed the baseline at every point of the current-voltage characteristic. Peak power density reached 1.12 watts per square centimetre (0.74 watts per square centimetre for the baseline cell), with an open-circuit voltage of 1.08 volts and an area-specific resistance of 0.18 ohm square centimetres at the operating temperature. At 0.7 volts the cell delivered a current density of 1.35 amperes per square centimetre, at a fuel utilisation of 65 %. Power values are means over 6 cells, and the standard deviation of peak power density was 0.05 watts per square centimetre. Peak power fell by 3.8 % over 500 hours of operation. The resistance gain assigns the improvement to the cathode: the cobalt-free composition kept the polarisation resistance of the conventional cathode while the thin electrolyte cut the ohmic share. Anode-supported cells of this construction deliver stack-level power density at the tested temperature on a cathode free of cobalt.

points: The network carries 42 kilometres of buried supply and return pipe.
Heat delivered to customers annually: 310 gigawatt-hours.
Estimated distribution loss for the network: 14 % of the heat generated.
Losses reported for comparable networks span 8 % to 18 % of heat generated.
Design temperatures: supply 95 degrees Celsius, return 55 degrees Celsius.
The oldest pipe sections have been in service for 38 years.
The logging campaign covers 26 substations over 12 months.
The loss model will report each section loss with an uncertainty of 2 percentage points.
definitions: distribution loss = the heat generated at the plant minus the heat metered at customer substations, stated as a share of the heat generated
uncertainty = the half-width of the interval within which the modelled loss for a network section is expected to lie
substation = the heat exchange station at which network heat passes to a building or a customer circuit
limits: The loss split applies to the pipe stock as surveyed; a section replaced during the campaign leaves the model at replacement.
prose:
District heating moves heat from a central plant to buildings through buried pipe, and the heat lost in transit is paid for at the plant and delivered nowhere. The network studied here carries 42 kilometres of buried supply and return pipe, delivers 310 gigawatt-hours of heat to customers annually, and runs at design temperatures of 95 degrees Celsius supply and 55 degrees Celsius return. The estimated distribution loss for the network is 14 % of the heat generated. Losses reported for comparable networks span 8 % to 18 % of heat generated, and the spread between networks of similar age and load reflects insulation state, burial depth, groundwater contact and return temperature discipline.
The network total is known from plant and customer metering. The split of the total among network sections is not known: no section of the network carries the flow and temperature logging that a section balance requires, and the oldest pipe sections have been in service for 38 years with insulation state recorded only at excavation. A replacement programme priced by section needs the split, ranked by loss per unit length, before capital follows the ranking. This study measures the split. Flow and temperature logging at 26 substations over 12 months feeds a section-by-section heat balance, calibrated against the metered network total. The loss model will report each section loss with an uncertainty of 2 percentage points, and sections will be ranked by loss per unit length with the uncertainty carried into the ranking. The loss split applies to the pipe stock as surveyed; a section replaced during the campaign leaves the model at replacement.

points: Sulphuric acid leaching in published laboratory studies recovers 92 % of the cobalt in black mass.
The published leaching conditions centre on an acid concentration of 2 moles per litre at 80 degrees Celsius.
Lithium recovery in the same published routes reaches 70 %.
The feed characterised in this study carries iron at 12 % by mass.
The leach test programme covers 5 feed grades.
Residence times in the leach tests extend to 4 hours.
Characterisation covers 3 industrial black mass samples.
definitions: black mass = the shredded and separated electrode material from spent lithium-ion batteries, carrying the cathode metals
leaching = the dissolution of target metals from a solid into a liquid phase
feed grade = the metal content class of a black mass batch, set by the battery chemistry of the source stream
limits: The programme addresses hydrometallurgical leaching only; pyrometallurgical pretreatment of the same feeds falls outside the study.
prose:
Spent lithium-ion batteries return to recyclers as black mass, and leaching moves the cathode metals from the black mass into a liquor that refining can separate. Sulphuric acid leaching in published laboratory studies recovers 92 % of the cobalt in black mass, and lithium recovery in the same published routes reaches 70 %. The published leaching conditions centre on an acid concentration of 2 moles per litre at 80 degrees Celsius, with a reductant added to bring cobalt into solution. The published record rests on single-chemistry feeds prepared for the laboratory: sorted cells of one cathode type, milled to a controlled size, with the fluorine and iron burden of a mixed industrial stream absent.
Industrial black mass arrives mixed. Cathode chemistries blend in the shredder, current collector fragments ride with the electrode material, and the feed characterised in this study carries iron at 12 % by mass. Recovery of cobalt and lithium from a mixed feed at the published conditions is not recorded, and the acid consumption of the impurity load is unrecorded; the gap sits in the transfer from a sorted laboratory feed to the stream a plant receives. This study measures that transfer. Characterisation covers 3 industrial black mass samples, spanning the grade range of the receiving stream. The leach test programme covers 5 feed grades drawn from the characterised samples, and residence times in the leach tests extend to 4 hours. Metal recovery, acid consumption and residue composition close each test, and recovery is reported against the characterised feed grade of the sample leached. The programme addresses hydrometallurgical leaching only; pyrometallurgical pretreatment of the same feeds falls outside the study.

points: Calibration standard: benzoic acid, mass 0.986 grams, certified energy of combustion 26434 joules per gram.
Temperature rise on combustion of the standard: 2.412 kelvin.
Fuse wire and acid formation corrections in the calibration totalled 61 joules.
Energy equivalent of the calorimeter: 10780 joules per kelvin.
The bomb was charged with oxygen at 3.0 megapascals.
Samples were dried at 105 degrees Celsius for 2 hours before pelleting.
The thermometer resolves 0.001 kelvin.
Calibration was repeated over 5 combustions; the standard deviation of the energy equivalent was 24 joules per kelvin.
Bomb temperature was recorded every 10 seconds through the firing and the after-period.
definitions: energy equivalent = the heat capacity of the calorimeter assembly, stated as the energy that raises the bomb and its contents by one kelvin
bomb calorimeter = a sealed constant-volume vessel in which a sample burns in oxygen and the released energy passes to the surrounding water jacket
after-period = the interval after combustion during which the temperature drift of the calorimeter is recorded for the cooling correction
limits: The calibration applies to the bomb, bucket and water charge as assembled; a change of water charge or bomb internals requires recalibration.
prose:
Energy of combustion was measured in a bomb calorimeter, a sealed constant-volume vessel in which the sample burns in oxygen and the released energy passes to the surrounding water jacket. Calibration preceded the sample programme and used benzoic acid as the standard. The calibration mass was 0.986 grams of benzoic acid, with a certified energy of combustion of 26434 joules per gram. The bomb was charged with oxygen at 3.0 megapascals, fired by a fuse wire, and the temperature rise on combustion of the standard was 2.412 kelvin. Bomb temperature was recorded every 10 seconds through the firing and the after-period, and the cooling correction came from the drift recorded in the after-period. Fuse wire and acid formation corrections in the calibration totalled 61 joules. The energy equivalent of the calorimeter was 10780 joules per kelvin. Calibration was repeated over 5 combustions, and the standard deviation of the energy equivalent was 24 joules per kelvin.
Samples were dried at 105 degrees Celsius for 2 hours before pelleting, and each pellet was weighed into the crucible immediately before the bomb closed. The thermometer resolves 0.001 kelvin, and the resolution sets the floor of the temperature-rise measurement against which the cooling correction is applied. Sample combustions followed the calibration sequence exactly: the same oxygen charge, the same water charge, the same firing circuit and the same correction set, with the energy of combustion of the sample calculated from the measured temperature rise and the energy equivalent of the calorimeter. The calibration applies to the bomb, bucket and water charge as assembled; a change of water charge or bomb internals requires recalibration before further samples are fired. Firing records for every combustion are retained with the sample record.

definitions: ICP = inductively coupled plasma, the ionised argon discharge that atomises and excites the sample in the spectrometer
detection limit = the lowest concentration the method reports, set at three times the standard deviation of blank digestions

prose:
Element concentrations in digested samples were measured by inductively coupled plasma (ICP) optical emission spectrometry, in which a nebulised sample solution enters an argon plasma and element concentrations are read from the emission spectrum of the plasma. Digestion came first. Each sample was weighed at 0.250 grams into a digestion vessel, the acid volume was 9 millilitres, and the cooled digest was diluted to 50 millilitres. A blank digestion accompanied every batch, and the batch blank carried the full acid and vessel sequence with no sample.
Plasma conditions held constant across the programme. The plasma gas flow was 15 litres per minute of argon, the auxiliary gas flow was 0.9 litres per minute, and the nebuliser gas flow was 0.7 litres per minute. Radio-frequency power applied to the plasma was 1300 watts. Cadmium was measured at the 228.8 nanometre emission line, and every element was read at a line free of overlap from the matrix elements at the concentrations present. Calibration used 5 standard levels: 0.05, 0.10, 0.50, 1.00 and 5.00 milligrams per litre, prepared in the same acid matrix as the digests. Yttrium served as internal standard, held at 2.00 milligrams per litre in every solution; sample signals were ratioed to the yttrium signal before the calibration applied, and the ratio corrects nebuliser drift during a run. The detection limit for cadmium was 0.003 milligrams per litre, set from 10 blank digestions. Spike recovery was 97 % at a spike level of 0.20 milligrams per litre, and a failed spike recovery stopped the batch for re-digestion. The rinse time between samples was 60 seconds. Concentrations above the highest calibration level were diluted and re-run; the calibration does not extend by extrapolation.

Void content was 0.8 % by volume, against 1.9 % by volume for the manufacturer cycle.

definitions: glass transition temperature = the temperature at which the cured resin passes from a glassy to a rubbery state, measured here by differential scanning calorimetry
interlaminar shear strength = the shear strength between plies of a laminate, measured in a short-beam bending test
void content = the volume fraction of enclosed gas in the cured laminate
limits: The claim covers panels at the tested thickness; sections above 12 millimetres were not tested.
One prepreg batch was tested; batch-to-batch variation and humidity ageing stand outside the trial.
prose:
The trial supports a shortened cure cycle for the tested panel construction, at the tested thickness and on the tested prepreg batch. The tested cycle ramped at 2 degrees Celsius per minute to a dwell at 180 degrees Celsius, held for 120 minutes, and total cycle time fell by 35 % against the manufacturer cycle. Laminates from the shortened cycle carried a glass transition temperature of 196 degrees Celsius. Interlaminar shear strength reached 78 megapascals (71 megapascals for the manufacturer cycle), and void content was 0.8 % by volume (1.9 % by volume for the manufacturer cycle). Flexural strength was 1240 megapascals, with a standard deviation of 45 megapascals across 8 coupons. Panel thickness in the trial was 4 millimetres.
The shortened cycle gains time in the ramp and holds the dwell at the manufacturer temperature, and the property set records no penalty for the gain: the slower ramp lets volatiles leave the lay-up before the resin gels, and the void content records the effect. The claim covers panels at the tested thickness; sections above 12 millimetres were not tested, and thick sections cure under an exotherm that the thin-panel trial does not reproduce. One prepreg batch was tested; batch-to-batch variation and humidity ageing stand outside the trial, and a production release needs both before the cycle replaces the manufacturer schedule in service parts. The autoclave programme as tested is ready for a repeat trial on a second prepreg batch, with the same coupon plan and the same acceptance values carried over from this trial.

The outlet concentration was recorded continuously at the bed exit. Breakthrough, defined at an outlet concentration reaching 5 % of the inlet concentration, occurred at a breakthrough time of 138 minutes (standard deviation 6 minutes across 3 replicate beds), and the saturation time was 210 minutes.

Temperature gradient through the wall: 60 kelvin per metre in magnitude.
Heat transfer rate from the evaluation: 1008 watts.
definitions: q = the heat transfer rate through the wall, in watts
k = the thermal conductivity of the wall material, in watts per metre kelvin
A = the wall area normal to the heat flow, in square metres
T = the temperature in the wall, in degrees Celsius
x = the distance through the wall, in metres, measured from the hot face
limits: The relation holds for steady one-dimensional conduction with constant thermal conductivity; at a zero temperature gradient the heat transfer rate is zero.
prose:
Heat conduction through a plane wall at steady state carries a heat transfer rate set by the material, the geometry and the temperature field in the wall. The heat transfer rate q, stated in watts, is the quantity the relation predicts: q is the energy crossing the wall per unit time. For the wall treated here, q equals the negative product of the thermal conductivity k, the wall area A and the temperature gradient dT/dx, the rate of change of temperature T with distance x through the wall. In the relation, k is the thermal conductivity of the wall material in watts per metre kelvin, A is the wall area normal to the heat flow in square metres, T is the temperature in degrees Celsius, and x is the distance through the wall in metres, measured from the hot face. The relation holds for steady, one-dimensional conduction with a thermal conductivity that does not vary with temperature, and a zero temperature gradient gives a zero heat transfer rate; a wall with a uniform temperature conducts no heat under the relation, at either face temperature.
The wall evaluated here has a thermal conductivity of 1.4 watts per metre kelvin, an area of 12 square metres and a thickness of 0.25 metres, with face temperatures of 20 degrees Celsius at the hot face and 5 degrees Celsius at the cold face. The temperature difference across the wall is 15 kelvin, and the temperature gradient through the wall is 60 kelvin per metre in magnitude. The heat transfer rate from the evaluation is 1008 watts, directed from the hot face toward the cold face. The negative sign in the relation carries that direction: temperature falls along the direction of the heat flow, and the gradient term records the fall.
